children: Richard Harris, Chief Executive of Port Shelter Investment Management, believes the latest tariff threat from US President Donald Trump is unlikely to have a significant impact on India.

He described the move as the last attempt by a lame-duck president to push through tariff measures, adding that markets are unlikely to take the latest announcement too seriously. Harris believes the tariff overhang should not be a major concern for investors.

However, he is more cautious about the outlook for global equities, particularly technology stocks riding the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Harris believes much of the optimism around AI has already been factored into stock prices, leaving limited room for further positive surprises.

He described the current market as a "cappuccino market", where there is some underlying value but considerable froth on the surface. He also flagged the sharp swings in stocks such as Nvidia as a sign of emotion-driven trading and growing volatility.

Looking ahead, Harris believes investors could face a more challenging period as markets struggle to find fresh triggers for growth. While he remains positive about AI's long-term potential, he cautioned that technology stocks may have borrowed too much performance from the future.

Drawing parallels with the dot-com boom of 2000, he warned that some stocks could take years to regain their highs after a correction. He expects early 2027 to be a particularly testing period for markets.

We know that in the past, the headline is seldom the final deal, but how worried should India be? And is this going to be a headwind?[/ques][ans]In terms of worry, basically not at all. This is the last gasp of a president who's failed in his other tariff measures. He is able to do this on this so-called capacity issue, but if you look at many of the countries that have been targeted, they don't really have a capacity issue at all, especially Europe. So it's really a last gasp, in my view, from Trump, and I don't think that people should really take it with much regard. He is a lame-duck president. He will try and push through as many of these stale issues and policies as he can, but I think markets are not really going to be taken in by this particular piece of news.[/ans][/faq][faq type="interview"][ques]What about the big sell-off? It was a 5% down day for the Nasdaq last night, and then we recovered. Looking at the price action, should we make something of it and draw conclusions that maybe this was the last flush and things could be cleaner now? Is positioning at least much cleaner?[/ques][ans]Calling it the last flush is a very brave thing to say. I think the volatility is quite concerning. It often portends some serious issues coming through. The one thing we have been missing in this whole bull rally of the AI bubble is a trigger that makes people think, “Hold on, maybe it isn't as good as we thought.” I've been calling these a cappuccino market because there is some value underneath, but, of course, there's an enormous amount of froth on top. I think prices have really been pushed ahead because of these behavioural issues. Take Nvidia as an example. On day one, its market capitalisation falls by nearly a trillion dollars. On day two, it rises by nearly a trillion dollars. These are very, very unusual movements driven purely by emotion and narrative. I think that's quite a dangerous foundation for investors to place their reliance on.[/ans][/faq][faq type="interview"][ques]Would you say that AI implementation still has a very long runway, but we're getting signs that these stock prices have factored in almost all the good news? If I look at the price action in Nvidia, it's one day up and one day down. Anthropic came out with its IP, and there was so much excitement. Looking at the correction from the top, do you think fatigue is setting into the AI trade and investment theme, and that it could actually start underperforming from next year?[/ques][ans]Fatigue is a very good word because we've had good news upon good news. We have to remember that it's all about expectations. Markets are about expectations, and these narratives are about expectations. It's not just growth that we need to think about because we are going to have tremendous underlying growth in AI. It's the growth on growth. It's that second-derivative growth that's important because it provides surprising expectations, and that's what drives markets forward. It's quite difficult to see where that second-derivative growth is really going to come from because so much good news is already in the market. We have to go back to the year 2000, to see a fairly strong parallel. We saw the internet coming in, and some companies gained enormous amounts of value. Even stocks like Amazon rose very sharply, but then it took them 15 or so years to recover their all-time highs. Amazon was a great stock, and everybody knew it was a great stock, but it still took that long to recover its all-time highs. What we've done is borrow an enormous amount of performance from the future, and we're probably going to give that back at some point, perhaps in the new year. People may start seeing different things when the Democrats come in and push through various issues. I think early 2027 is going to be a real testing time.[/ans][/faq]

title: Trump tariff threat unlikely to shake markets; AI stock valuations a concern: Richard Harris
